implementation_notes: Jakarta Persistence maps the hierarchy declaratively: @Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.SINGLE_TABLE) on the root entity, @DiscriminatorColumn(name=..., length=...) to configure the type column, and @DiscriminatorValue on each entity - and because SINGLE_TABLE is also the default when no strategy is declared, a hierarchy can end up in one wide table without a single annotation saying so. The provider (Hibernate and friends) generates the union of columns, makes subtype columns nullable and appends the discriminator predicate to entity queries, so the generated mapper/EntityManager replaces hand-written mapping code. The classic manual form remains common in JDBC/MyBatis codebases: one row class per table plus a factory switching on the type column.
pitfalls: The strategy is declared once on the root entity and cannot vary per subclass; forgetting @Inheritance silently selects SINGLE_TABLE, so a schema meant to be JOINED is created as one wide table.
Subtype columns are generated as nullable, so subtype invariants must be expressed with Bean Validation or CHECK constraints - the provider will not enforce them.
The discriminator defaults to DTYPE/STRING: schema reviews and data migrations must know the real column name and the per-class values, or reports and raw SQL will look for the wrong column.
Because all columns live in one row there is no per-subtype lazy loading; fetch plans cannot avoid the wide row, only avoid loading it at all.
